issues.description: The introduction explicitly states that all three interventions will be placed BEFORE the collaborative recall phase, framing them as inoculation against incoming misinformation. The methods and procedure section, however, places the interventions AFTER the collaborative recall and a second filler task, immediately before the individual memory test. These two placements are not equivalent: pre-collaborative-recall placement could alter the social dynamics of the discussion itself (e.g., participants may challenge each other differently), whereas post-collaborative-recall placement functions solely as a post-warning before the memory test. The entire theoretical rationale built on IMP and informational influence is developed assuming participants have already been exposed to misinformation when the intervention acts. The contradiction makes it impossible to determine what study was actually designed and what theoretical claims are being tested.
issues.quote: Introduction: 'What is important, we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase (that is, before exposing participants to misinformation).' Methods 2.5: 'The procedure will consist of four main phases: (1) presenting the original material, (2) collaborative recall (including misinformation), (3) three procedures to reduce vulnerability to misinformation (and a control condition), and (4) an individual memory test of the original material.'

issues.description: The procedure section describes the individual memory test as consisting of open-ended questions with four derived scoring indices (correct, misinformation-consistent, other, and total). The analysis plan section then describes using a two-alternative forced-choice format for the same test. These are fundamentally different response formats: open-ended responses can yield 'other' and 'don't know' answers, while forced-choice constrains responses to two options and cannot produce 'other' responses. The four-index scoring system explicitly mentioned for the ANOVA analysis is only possible with open-ended responses. Yet the analysis plan simultaneously describes the two-alternative forced-choice scoring logic used in prior MORI studies. This contradiction makes it impossible to determine the actual test format, the valid scoring procedure, or what prior effect sizes are relevant benchmarks.
issues.quote: Procedure: 'The test will contain 20 open-ended questions, eight of which will cover all the critical details included in the movie.' Analysis plan: 'In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.'

issues.description: The power analysis treats 240 participants as 240 independent observations for all sample-size calculations, but the design section states that 'pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups,' making the pair—not the individual—the unit of randomization. With 120 pairs divided among four groups, the effective sample for between-subjects comparisons is 30 pairs per group, not 60 individuals per group. All power estimates, required sample sizes, and the conclusion that '240 participants allows for excellent power to detect medium and large effects' are therefore inflated by approximately a factor of two. The required n of 82 for a medium pairwise interaction effect refers to individual participants under independence assumptions; with 30 pairs per group (60 per two-group comparison), power for the primary hypothesis is substantially lower than claimed.
issues.quote: Considering the accessible financial, organizational and time resources, a sample of 240 participants was assumed; this allows for excellent power to detect medium and large effect sizes but not small ones. [...] Pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups.

issues.description: The planned two-factor ANOVA treats individual participants as the unit of analysis, violating the independence assumption. Each pair member is the direct source of misinformation for the other during the collaborative recall; consequently, the memory error scores of the two pair members are statistically dependent. For any given critical item, both Participant A's and Participant B's responses are shaped by the same dyadic conversation. Applying standard ANOVA to these nested observations produces anti-conservative F-tests with inflated Type I error rates for between-subjects effects. The appropriate analytical approach would involve multilevel modeling with pairs as a clustering variable, or aggregating to pair-level outcomes for between-subjects tests. This issue is distinct from the unit-of-randomization problem and compounds it.
issues.quote: The results will be analyzed by means of a two-factor ANOVA, with one within-subjects factor with two levels (discussed vs. non-discussed items) and one between-subjects factor with four levels (three groups of methods of reducing memory conformity and the control group).

issues.description: The design section claims that 'discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced,' implying that which of the eight critical details are discussed versus not discussed varies systematically across participants or pairs. However, the procedure section explicitly states that 'each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase.' If the discussion set is fixed and identical across all pairs, full counterbalancing is impossible. The discussed vs. non-discussed distinction would be entirely confounded with item identity—any observed accuracy difference could reflect item-specific properties (inherent memorability, salience, visual distinctiveness) rather than the effect of misinformation exposure. This undermines the central within-subjects comparison on which the entire study rests.
issues.quote: Design: 'In the study, the memory conformity effect will be measured in a within-subjects design and discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced.' Procedure: 'In order to ensure sufficient discussion, each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase.'

issues.description: The power analysis specifies a within-subjects correlation of r = 0.07 between repeated measures (discussed vs. non-discussed items), reportedly derived from two prior studies. This value is implausibly low for within-subjects memory data, where correlations typically range from r = 0.30 to r = 0.60 or higher. A near-zero correlation provides almost no statistical advantage over a between-subjects design and is inconsistent with the expectation that individuals with good overall memory for the film would score higher on both discussed and non-discussed items. It is likely that r = 0.07 represents a correlation between two other variables in the cited studies (e.g., a correlation coefficient for a regression analysis) rather than the test-retest correlation of the two within-subjects conditions. The basis for this estimate is not transparently documented, making independent verification of the power calculations impossible.
issues.quote: A correlation r = 0.07 between repeated measures was assumed based on the research described above (Ito et al., 2019; Kękuś et al., 2020). The option used in G*Power was 'ANOVA: Repeated measures, within-between'.

issues.description: The Demonstration and motivation condition includes a DRM procedure after which participants are explicitly told 'You were fooled. These words are strongly associated with the sets I read, but they were not included in them.' This deception revelation, which occurs before the individual MORI memory test, is unique to this condition and may cause participants to become suspicious that the main experiment also involved deception—which it does, since they watched different movie versions. This heightened meta-deception awareness is a condition-specific confound: participants may scrutinize both their own memories and the collaborative recall content differently than those in other conditions, not because of the intended motivational mechanism but because they have been primed to expect experimental deception. Any condition differences could thus reflect differential awareness of the MORI manipulation rather than genuine resistance to conformity.
issues.quote: 'Thank you for completing this memory task. Please take a look at your sheets now. See if you have written down any of the words: doctor, window, sweet, thief. If so, you were fooled. These words are strongly associated with the sets I read, but they were not included in them. You can see how easily human memory can be distorted'.

issues.description: The analysis plan specifies four separate ANOVA analyses on four different scoring indices from the individual memory test (correct answers, misinformation-consistent answers, other answers, total answers), plus accuracy comparisons across filler, discussed, and non-discussed items. No primary outcome is designated; no correction for multiple comparisons is specified (e.g., Bonferroni, false discovery rate, or a multivariate MANOVA approach). This creates a substantial multiple-testing problem: across four indices and multiple planned comparisons, the family-wise Type I error rate is far above the nominal 0.05. Additionally, the prediction that 'Demonstration and motivation > Extended Warning > Education > Control' is stated verbally but the analysis plan does not specify pre-planned contrast weights or a formal ordered-hypothesis test (e.g., Williams trend test), leaving the assessment of ordered effects underpowered and ambiguous.
issues.quote: We will explore the individual memory test's scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers.

issues.description: The exclusions section specifies only one exclusion criterion: technical problems during the session. Absent are criteria for: (1) participants who correctly identify the MORI deception during or after the study; (2) participants who already knew their partner, which could substantially alter conformity dynamics; (3) participants in the Demonstration and motivation condition who do not falsely recall any DRM lures (the key demonstration fails for them); (4) participants who looked over or around the polarized glasses; (5) participants with prior exposure to the MORI technique, misinformation effect research, or the specific stimuli; (6) pairs where one or both members did not reach the minimum age criterion. Leaving these unspecified introduces researcher degrees of freedom for post-hoc exclusions that could materially affect results, and prevents independent replication of the exact protocol.
issues.quote: 3.1. Exclusions: We will exclude participants in the case of any technical problems during the experimental session.

issues.description: The manuscript contains no mention of experimenter blinding to condition. In this study, the experimenter directly interacts with participants across conditions (administering the DRM procedure, delivering personalized verbal feedback about false recalls, running all sessions). Unblinded experimenters can inadvertently convey demand characteristics through tone, pacing, or emphasis. This concern is especially acute for the Demonstration and motivation condition, where the experimenter verbally delivers the deception revelation and motivation speech, and for the debriefing, where experimenter behavior could differ based on knowledge of condition assignment. No mention is made of standardized scripts, audio-recorded delivery to ensure consistency, or any other safeguard against experimenter expectancy effects.
issues.quote: At this moment in this group, the experimenter will give the following information to the participants: 'Thank you for completing this memory task. Please take a look at your sheets now. See if you have written down any of the words: doctor, window, sweet, thief.'

issues.description: The analysis plan first specifies a nuanced rule: if a partner provides an answer consistent with what the participant saw (e.g., guessing correctly), that item is NOT classified as containing misinformation and should not be scored as a misleading trial. However, the very next paragraph contradicts this by stating 'we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner's differing version of events.' These two rules are mutually incompatible: the first is item-specific and condition-dependent; the second is categorical and ignores actual discussion content. Applying the categorical rule inflates the misinformation exposure count by including cases where no misinformation was actually introduced, attenuating the observed conformity effect and biasing analyses of its reduction.
issues.quote: 'However, if the partner provided an answer consistent with what the participant had seen, that is, "white mug" (such a situation can happen, e.g., as a result of the partner's guessing), the situation will not be classified as misleading.' vs. 'we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner's differing version of events.'

issues.description: The validity of the entire MORI paradigm depends on participants remaining unaware that they watched different movie versions during the collaborative recall. If participants realize this, misinformation is no longer attributed to an informational authority (a co-witness who saw the same thing) but to a known source of discrepant information, fundamentally changing the conformity dynamic and the applicability of the informational influence and IMP mechanisms. The only check described is a post-test purpose awareness question during debriefing, which occurs after the individual memory test and therefore cannot be used to exclude contaminated data or differentiate trials. No check is administered immediately after the collaborative recall, and no pre-specified exclusion threshold for MORI awareness is defined.
issues.quote: Next, the subjects will be requested to say what they think the real purpose of the study was. Their responses will be recorded for exploratory analysis of any relationship between hypothesis awareness and performance.

issues.description: The authors categorically exclude normative influence from consideration, arguing that because participants work individually without real-time comparison, there is 'no cost of disagreeing.' This conflates the absence of concurrent social presence with the absence of normative motivation. Internalized social norms from the prior discussion persist during private testing; participants may feel interpersonal obligation to the partner with whom they just conversed, anticipate post-study comparison of answers, or experience discomfort at the thought of contradicting someone face-to-face. Empirical research on private conformity (e.g., Deutsch & Gerard, 1955) establishes precisely that normative influence operates even absent direct observation. Dismissing this as 'completely ruled out' is theoretically unjustifiable and leads the authors to attribute all conformity effects to informational influence, which then restricts their predictions about which interventions should work and for whom—potentially producing incorrect hypotheses.
issues.quote: Given the fact that the individual memory test does not include any element of direct interpersonal pressure, we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody, therefore there is no cost of disagreeing.

issues.description: The primary operationalization of memory conformity is the accuracy difference between discussed and non-discussed critical items. However, this difference does not uniquely index memory conformity. Discussed items differ from non-discussed items not only in misinformation exposure but also in the additional processing that occurs during discussion (elaboration, verbal encoding, potential interference). A participant who simply forgets a discussed item and guesses would show lower accuracy on discussed relative to non-discussed items—producing the signature conformity pattern—without any conformity process. The measure that genuinely captures conformity is the proportion of misinformation-consistent responses on discussed items relative to non-discussed items, which the analysis plan lists as one of four indices but not as the primary conformity measure used to define intervention efficacy.
issues.quote: The efficacy of a given method will be confirmed if the magnitude of memory conformity (expressed as the difference between the accuracy on discussed and non-discussed items) is smaller in the group in which this method was applied than in the control group.

issues.description: The criterion for establishing intervention efficacy is a reduced accuracy gap between discussed and non-discussed items in the intervention group relative to the control group. This gap can narrow via two mechanistically distinct pathways: (1) accuracy on discussed items increases (the intended effect—participants resist misinformation), or (2) accuracy on non-discussed items decreases (an unintended harm—the intervention somehow disrupts memory for non-contaminated content, perhaps by inducing general uncertainty or distrust of memory). The analysis plan does not pre-specify examination of main effects on each item type separately, nor does it pre-specify a criterion distinguishing 'real improvement' from 'collateral harm.' A significant interaction cannot be interpreted as demonstrating resistance to misinformation without ruling out the second pathway.
issues.quote: The efficacy of a given method will be confirmed if the magnitude of memory conformity (expressed as the difference between the accuracy on discussed and non-discussed items) is smaller in the group in which this method was applied than in the control group.

issues.description: The Extended Warning condition involves a podcast on 'the fallibility of human memory,' including 'the misinformation effect, source misattribution, and the influence of a lack of confidence on memory reports.' The Education about memory condition involves a podcast discussing 'the mechanisms of memory, in particular its constructive nature' and the Seven Sins of Memory. The authors acknowledge 'some overlap between the three interventions,' but this overlap appears substantial: both conditions provide information about memory fallibility via podcast, and the Demonstration and motivation condition also includes a podcast on memory mechanisms. The conditions are not experimentally orthogonal and differ primarily in framing rather than content. If the conditions produce similar results, it is impossible to determine whether this reflects a genuine equivalence of mechanisms or simply that the three conditions delivered indistinguishable manipulations. No manipulation check assessing condition-specific knowledge acquisition or attitude change is planned.
issues.quote: Secondly, we are aware of some overlap between the three interventions, for instance, teaching about memory is included is present in a way in both Education about memory and Demonstration and motivation.

issues.description: The Integrative Framework for Memory and Performance (Blank, 1998) was explicitly developed for the classic paradigm in which misinformation is delivered impersonally via written narrative. The authors acknowledge this limitation but assert that 'similar processes may apply to the memory conformity paradigm' without providing empirical evidence, formal argument, or citation of prior theoretical work supporting the extension. Social conformity paradigms differ from classic misinformation paradigms along multiple dimensions: source monitoring requirements differ (person vs. text), the misinformation is bidirectional (each witness misleads the other simultaneously), social-relational motivations are engaged, and the timing and salience of the discrepant information differ. Simply restating IMP predictions as if they straightforwardly transfer to a fundamentally different paradigm is a theoretical leap that is not justified in the manuscript.
issues.quote: The IMP was developed in the context of the classic misinformation paradigm, in which the post-event information is delivered impersonally. However, similar processes may apply to the memory conformity paradigm.

issues.description: The Demonstration and motivation condition's core mechanism depends on participants falsely recalling at least one DRM critical lure so the experimenter can demonstrate vulnerability to influence. DRM false recall is not universal, however; some participants correctly withhold critical lures, particularly with short lists or high metacognitive awareness. For participants who produce no false recalls, the demonstrative core of the manipulation fails entirely, yet no contingency is described. Including non-demonstrable participants in the analysis would attenuate the condition effect by diluting the manipulation. Excluding them post-hoc would introduce non-random attrition (participants who are already more resistant to suggestion would be disproportionately removed from the most active intervention condition), systematically biasing comparisons. A pre-specified rule for handling DRM non-responders is absent.
issues.quote: The DRM procedure usually results in most of the participants falsely recalling at least a few of the critical lures. [...] The results will be fed back to participants in order to demonstrate to them that their memory was vulnerable to a subtle influence.

issues.description: The procedure specifies that all collaborative recall discussions will be audio recorded, which implies these data will be analyzed. However, no analysis plan whatsoever is provided for the recordings. It is unspecified whether they will be transcribed, coded for behavioral indicators (e.g., rate of disagreement, explicit misinformation introduction, capitulation behaviors), or simply stored. Without a pre-specified coding scheme, reliability procedure, or analysis plan, these data constitute an undisclosed degree of freedom: they could be analyzed post-hoc to explain unexpected results or support any pattern of findings across conditions. The mere mention of audio recording without corresponding analysis pre-registration is inconsistent with the registered-report format of the manuscript.
issues.quote: Each question and its five possible responses will be displayed in a PowerPoint presentation for 60 seconds while participants discuss the answer. If the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented. The discussion will be audio recorded.

issues.description: The power analysis derives a joint effect size (Hedges' g = 1.13) from a random-effects meta-analysis of only two studies with dramatically different effect sizes (g = 1.92, N = 55 and g = 0.38, N = 74). The authors acknowledge the large discrepancy and appropriately adopt a random-effects model, but report neither I², the Q-statistic, τ², nor the 95% confidence interval around the joint estimate. With only two studies producing an effect-size range spanning 1.54 g units, the between-study variance is enormous and the joint estimate is highly imprecise. The wide confidence interval would substantially alter power calculations if the true effect is closer to g = 0.38. Without heterogeneity statistics, readers cannot evaluate the reliability of the effect size used to power the replication component of the study.
issues.quote: Given the rather large difference in effect sizes between both studies, random effects were assumed while calculating the joint effect size, which was 1.13. This amounts to a Cohen f of about 0.57.

issues.description: The analysis plan includes an exploratory analysis in which DRM procedure performance will be used 'as a possible predictor of the results on the MORI technique.' This analysis is not pre-specified beyond a single sentence: no specific outcome variable, regression model, covariate structure, or hypothesis is stated. This leaves the analysis entirely open-ended, allowing post-hoc selection of the specific DRM measure, the specific MORI outcome, the direction of the prediction, and the statistical test used. In a registered report context, including such an underspecified analysis creates a gap through which selective reporting could occur without technically violating the registered analysis plan.
issues.quote: As an additional exploratory analysis, the results on the DRM procedure will be used as a possible predictor of the results on the MORI technique.

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly frames its contributions in terms of forensic practice, eyewitness testimony accuracy, and reducing wrongful convictions. However, the sample is restricted to adults aged 16–35 recruited via internet and media advertisements, yielding a sample that is almost certainly young, digitally literate, and likely predominantly university-educated. Real forensic witness populations include elderly individuals, people with low literacy, individuals under acute stress, and witnesses to unexpected rather than staged events. The age restriction, while procedurally motivated, produces a sample with systematically higher baseline cognitive resources and lower susceptibility to suggestion than many forensic witness populations. This fundamental mismatch between the sample and the forensic application context is not acknowledged as a limitation.
issues.quote: erroneous testimonies continue to be the leading cause of incorrect court judgments [...] The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet.
